title: Interview frame
summary: Spend the hour in a fixed order and leave time to name the bottleneck.

body:
Rule. Run a system-design hour in a fixed beat order: clarify what the product must do, agree on scale, sketch the external API, sketch the data, draw one read path and one write path, then pick a single bottleneck and go deep. State assumptions out loud and move. Ask before inventing a feature the prompt never required. Stop when a box has no number and no failure story — that box is the next dive.

Why it matters. Candidates either drown in boxes or freeze on the first database brand. Interviewers grade the order and the tradeoffs more than the ink volume. A frame keeps twenty minutes for the hard part instead of spending fifty on a logo farm.

Worked example. Prompt: design a URL shortener. Minute 0–5: confirm create short link, redirect by code, optional custom alias; ask about auth and analytics and park them if not required. Minute 5–10: assume 100 million new links per month ≈ 40 writes/sec average, 10× read:write → about 400 redirects/sec; store roughly 100M × 100 bytes ≈ 10 GB plus indexes. Minute 10–20: POST /links returns code; GET /{code} redirects. Table links(code PK, url, created_at). Minute 20–35: write inserts row; read is PK lookup, optionally cached. Minute 35–50: deep dive on code generation collision handling and cache invalidation on delete. You never drew Kafka in minute three.

When to use. Use this frame for every greenfield system prompt. Use it to restart politely when the conversation jumps to sharding before requirements exist. Use the "no number, no failure story" test to choose the next deep dive.

When to refuse. Refuse diving into a vendor or a queue before the API and data are named. Refuse inventing multi-region DR when the prompt is a single-region MVP. Refuse spending the hour on every possible feature. Refuse a design where no bottleneck was ever named.
